id: formal bug report with stack trace and package manifest#1
in:
Our ingest worker started crashing in production about four hours after we shipped release 2.14.0. It runs fine locally and it ran fine in staging for a full day under synthetic load, so whatever this is, it depends on something about the production data or the production environment that we are not reproducing.

The process exits with a non-zero code roughly every ninety seconds, the supervisor restarts it, it chews through part of the queue and then dies again. We have lost about eleven thousand messages so far because the retry topic is also filling up. Here is the trace we get on every crash, it is identical each time apart from the offset in the last frame:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toISOString')
    at normalizeEvent (/srv/ingest/dist/pipeline/normalize.js:142:38)
    at /srv/ingest/dist/pipeline/batch.js:87:22
    at Array.map (<anonymous>)
    at processBatch (/srv/ingest/dist/pipeline/batch.js:86:31)
    at async Worker.handle (/srv/ingest/dist/worker.js:203:5)
    at async Runner.loop (/srv/ingest/dist/runner.js:64:9)
```

The line it dies on reads `const stamp = event.occurredAt.toISOString()` so clearly some events are arriving without an occurredAt, which we thought was impossible because the producer sets it. We have not changed the producer in six weeks.

Dependencies from the release, in case one of these is the actual culprit:

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@app/schema": "4.2.1",
    "kafkajs": "2.2.4",
    "pino": "9.5.0",
    "zod": "3.23.8"
  }
}
```

The only thing that moved in 2.14.0 was a bump of @app/schema from 4.1.9 to 4.2.1 and a change to how we batch, we went from batches of 50 to batches of 500. I suspect the schema bump but I cannot see how a schema package would strip a field. What would you look at first, and is there anything I should capture off the box before we roll back and lose the evidence?

in:
Dropping it would fix the sync and break whatever query it was added for, so it is worth spending ten minutes before you do that.

A GIN index on jsonb is expensive to update, and by default Postgres buffers those updates in a pending list that gets flushed periodically, which makes the cost arrive in lumps rather than evenly. Check whether `fastupdate` is on for that index and what `gin_pending_list_limit` is set to.

Batching the upserts into groups of 500 with a single multi-row insert and an `on conflict` clause would cut round trips by a factor of 500, and the index maintenance would still happen but you would stop paying per-statement overhead 31 thousand times. That fix helps whether or not the index stays.

We sell scheduling software to independent restaurants. The constraint from our side is that the legal team will not let us say anything about time saved unless we can point to a study, and we do not have one, so no percentages and no claims about hours back per week. We can say what the software does and we can describe the situation the customer is in.

Can you draft two versions, one that keeps a short founder paragraph and one that drops it entirely, so I can put both in front of the team and let them argue about it.

We want to partition the ledger table by month. Here is the plan I sketched out, tell me where it falls apart.

Step one, create the partitioned table `ledger_entries_partitioned` with the same columns and monthly range partitions covering the last four years plus twelve months ahead. Step two, add a trigger on the old table that copies every insert into the new one so they stay in sync. Step three, backfill the four years of history in chunks of 50k rows with a rake task we run manually from a one-off dyno. Step four, once the backfill is caught up, take a two minute write pause, rename both tables, drop the trigger. Step five, delete the old table a week later once we are confident.

My worries in order: the backfill is going to take days at 50k a chunk and I do not know how to make that safe to interrupt and resume. The rename in step four feels like the moment everything breaks and I cannot picture how to roll it back if the app comes up pointing at a half-populated table. And I have no idea what the six ledger-touching Sidekiq jobs do during the write pause, some of them run every minute.

Also our reporting follower has queries against `ledger_entries` that nobody on the team wrote and I am not sure who owns.

in:
Hello, I have problem with my docker setup since two weeks and my colleague also cannot understand it, so maybe you can help me. Sorry if my explanation is not so clear.

The situation is like this. We have small application, is a Python API with a worker and a Postgres, and everything works perfect on my machine and on my colleague machine also. But when we deploy to the server of the customer, the worker container it starts and after maybe 30 seconds it stops, no error message, exit code 0. Not 1, is 0, which I find very strange because for me exit 0 means it finished normally? But it should never finish, it should run forever and wait for jobs.

On the server the docker version is older, is 20.10 something, and on our machines we have 24. I don't know if this is important but I mention it.

This is our compose file, I removed the passwords:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    command: uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    depends_on:
      - db
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://app:REDACTED@db:5432/app
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379/0
  worker:
    build: .
    command: celery -A app.worker worker --loglevel=info
    depends_on:
      - db
      - cache
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://app:REDACTED@db:5432/app
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379/0
  db:
    image: postgres:15
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: REDACTED
      POSTGRES_DB: app
  cache:
    image: redis:7
volumes:
  pgdata:
```

What we tried already: we added restart: always to the worker, then it restarts in loop forever every 30 seconds which is not better, just more noise in the logs. We tried to run the same command with docker run manually on the server and then it works and stays running, which makes no sense to me because is the same image and same command.

Also when I do docker compose logs worker I see the celery banner and it prints ready, and then nothing, and then the container is gone. There is no traceback anywhere. My colleague thinks is OOM but the server has 16GB and nothing else runs there, and I think if OOM the exit code would be 137 not 0.

Do you have idea what to look for? I am not so experienced with docker so maybe is something obvious that I don't see.

We are adding webhooks to our public API and I want to get the payload shape right before anyone depends on it, because once customers write handlers against it we are stuck with it more or less forever.

id: four-turn api design discussion with mixed prose and snippets#2
in:
Both camps are right about different failure modes, and the tiebreaker is usually which mistake you can walk back.

A thin payload can grow into a fat one later without breaking anyone: adding fields is additive. A fat payload cannot shrink, because someone is reading every field you ship, including the ones you regret.

The staleness point is real and it is not a matter of taste. Delivery is retried, sometimes hours later, and a payload delivered at 14:00 describing state as of 13:12 will be treated as current by a naive handler. If you ship the object, ship it with the version or timestamp it describes so a handler can tell.

The permissions point is the one I would weigh heaviest. A webhook endpoint is a different trust boundary from your API, and reusing your internal serializer there is how fields leak.

Version the envelope, not the type. If versioning lives in the type name you end up with `invoice.finalized.v2` and every consumer has to subscribe twice during a migration, and your event catalog doubles. An envelope version lets a consumer pin one number and lets you serve two shapes off one subscription.

Deletes are the case where the thin payload genuinely fails, so treat them as the exception rather than reworking the rule. For a delete event, inline the fields a handler needs to act on — the id, whatever they key their local record by, and the deletion timestamp. A handler that receives `customer.deleted` needs enough to find its own row, and nothing else.
